topics.title: Topic 1: Critical Section Problem, Race Conditions & Essential Requirements

questions.source: 2021 Spring MC3 & 2022 Spring MC23 & 2023 Spring MC21
questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about a **race condition** is **TRUE**?

options.label: A
options.text: A race condition will result only if the outcome of execution does not depend on the order in which instructions are executed.

options.label: B
options.text: A race condition results when several threads try to access the same data concurrently without modifying it.

options.label: C
options.text: A race condition results when several threads try to access and modify the same shared data concurrently.

questions.explanation: A race condition requires concurrent access **and modification** of shared data, where the outcome depends on the execution order. Concurrent reading alone does not produce a race condition.

questions.source: 2021 Fall MC23 & 2021 Spring MC2 & 2025 Spring MC23
questions.prompt: A valid solution to the critical-section problem does **NOT** have to satisfy which of the following requirements?
questions.explanation: The three requirements are **mutual exclusion**, **progress**, and **bounded waiting**. Atomicity is a property of the hardware operations used to implement synchronization, not a required property of the solution itself.

questions.answer:
**9, 10, and 11.**

1. **10** — Thread 1 runs completely ($10 \rightarrow 11$), then Thread 2 runs completely ($11 \rightarrow 10$).
2. **11** — both threads read 10. Thread 2 writes 9, then Thread 1 writes its register value 11.
3. **9** — both threads read 10. Thread 1 writes 11, then Thread 2 writes its register value 9.

The solution key lists **-6, -9, 2, and 4**.

- Thread 2 runs to completion, then Thread 1: Thread 2 sets `a = 13`, `b = 10`, `c = 2`. Thread 1 then sets `a = 11` and `c = 11 - 10 = 1`.
- Thread 1 runs to completion, then Thread 2: Thread 1 sets `a = 4` and `c = 1`. Thread 2 then sets `c = 2`, so the final value is 2.
- Thread 1 computes `a = 4`, Thread 2 sets `b = 10`, and Thread 1 then evaluates `c = 4 - 10 = -6`.
- Other interleavings in the walkthrough also produce 1 and 3, depending on which write to `a`, `b`, or `c` happens last.

topics.title: Topic 2: Hardware Synchronization Support & Atomic Primitives

questions.answer:
**Mutual exclusion** is violated.

1. $P_i$ leaves its critical section, finds $P_j$ waiting, and sets `lock = false`.
2. Before $P_i$ executes `waiting[j] = false`, a third process $P_k$ that is spinning on `test_and_set(&lock)` sees the lock free, acquires it, and enters the critical section.
3. $P_i$ then sets `waiting[j] = false`. $P_j$ leaves its wait loop and also enters the critical section.
4. $P_k$ and $P_j$ are in their critical sections at the same time.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements regarding **spinlocks** is **FALSE**?

options.label: B
options.text: Spinlocks are useful in both single-processor and multiprocessor systems.

options.label: C
options.text: Spinlocks are effective when the lock is held by a running process on another CPU core.

options.label: D
options.text: Spinlocks waste CPU cycles during waiting.

questions.explanation: On a single processor, a process spinning on the CPU keeps the lock holder from running and releasing the lock. Spinlocks are useful on multiprocessors, where the holder can run on another core.

questions.source: 2021 Fall MC24 & 2022 Spring MC24 & 2023 Spring MC24
questions.prompt: When semaphores protect a critical section, a process normally calls `wait(S)` before entering and `signal(S)` after leaving. What can happen if a process reverses that order, calling `signal(S)` first and then `wait(S)`?

options.label: C
options.text: Multiple processes could be executing in their critical sections at the same time.

options.label: D
options.text: The calling process will get stuck immediately.

questions.explanation: Calling `signal(S)` first increments the semaphore (for example from 1 to 2). Another process can then pass `wait(S)` and enter its critical section at the same time, so mutual exclusion is lost.
$S_1$ must start at 1 so $T_1$ can pass `wait(S1)` immediately. $S_2$ and $S_3$ must start at 0 so $T_2$ and $T_3$ block until $T_1$ and $T_2$ signal them.

questions.answer:
`abcd`, `bacd`, and `bcad`.

$B$ must `signal(X)` before $A$ can pass `wait(X)` and print `b`. `a` is printed after that signal. `signal(Y)` in $A$ is what lets the later `wait(Y)` calls proceed, so `c` and `d` come after `b`.

- `abcd`: $B$ prints `a`, $A$ prints `b`, $A$ signals $Y$, $A$ prints `c`, $B$ prints `d`.
- `bacd`: $A$ prints `b`, $B$ prints `a`, then `c`, then `d`.
- `bcad`: $A$ prints `b`, signals $Y$, prints `c`, then $B$ prints `a` and `d`.

The code above is the completed FCFS readers-writers solution.

Semaphore `w` makes arriving readers and writers queue in first-come, first-served order. While a writer waits on `w`, later readers also block at `wait(w)` instead of passing the writer, so writers do not starve.

- **Blank 1**: `L.acquire();`
